question.text: Does positron emission tomography change management in primary rectal cancer?
question.context: The influence of positron emission tomography in the management of recurrent rectal cancer is well established but its role in primary rectal cancer remains uncertain. This study therefore prospectively assesses the impact of position emission tomography scanning on the management of primary rectal cancer. Forty-six patients with advanced primary rectal cancer referred for consideration of adjuvant preoperative therapy underwent position emission tomography scanning. The referring physicians prospectively recorded each patient's stage following conventional imaging and the proposed treatment plan prior to position emission tomography scanning. This was then compared with subsequent stage and actual management implemented, and the appropriateness of position emission tomography-induced changes was noted by subsequent clinical follow-up. The surgical management of 36 of 46 patients (78 percent) was unchanged as a result of position emission tomography, even though position emission tomography upstaged disease in 3 of 36 cases (8 percent) and downstaged disease in 5 of 36 cases (14 percent). In 8 of 46 cases (17 percent), management was altered because of the position emission tomography scan findings, including 6 cases (13 percent) in which surgery was cancelled and 2 other cases (4 percent) in which the radiotherapy field was changed. Where available, follow-up confirmed the appropriateness of position emission tomography-induced management change in each case. Two patients had a change in therapy independent of the position emission tomography scan due to clinical circumstances. Overall tumor stage was changed following position emission tomography in 18 of 46 patients (39 percent).

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found that position emission tomography (PET) scans did not significantly change the surgical management of most patients with advanced primary rectal cancer. While PET scans did upstage or downstage disease in some cases, the management was often unchanged. This suggests that PET scans are not routinely changing the management of primary rectal cancer.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The surgical management of 36 of 46 patients (78 percent) was unchanged as a result of position emission tomography, even though position emission tomography upstaged disease in 3 of 36 cases (8 percent) and downstaged disease in 5 of 36 cases (14 percent).
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While the study mentions that PET scans can upstage or downstage disease, the fact that management was often unchanged suggests that the scans are not routinely altering the treatment plan. Other factors, such as patient comorbidities or tumor characteristics, may be more influential in determining management decisions.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study shows that while PET scanning altered management in 17% of cases, the majority (78%) had unchanged surgical plans. The changes were appropriate in all cases where they occurred, but the overall impact on primary rectal cancer management remains uncertain due to the relatively small sample size and the fact that most patients did not experience management changes.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The study found that 39% of patients had their tumor stage changed by PET, but only 17% had actual management changes, indicating that while PET provides valuable information, it doesn't consistently alter primary treatment plans.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: The key differential is whether PET significantly changes primary treatment versus its established role in recurrent disease. The data suggests PET has limited impact on primary rectal cancer management compared to its established role in recurrent cases.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: Although 78% of patients had unchanged management, 17% experienced a change in management due to PET findings, including cancellation of surgery or modification of radiotherapy, and follow-up confirmed the appropriateness of these changes. This demonstrates that PET does influence management in a clinically significant subset of patients, even if not universally.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: In 8 of 46 cases (17%), management was altered because of PET scan findings, and follow-up confirmed the appropriateness of these changes.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: The option 'no' was considered but ruled out because PET did change management in 17% of cases. 'Maybe' was considered but less appropriate given the confirmed clinical impact of PET-induced changes in a measurable subset.
